message: The Titanic data has a binary target (Survived) and mixed numeric/categorical features. High‑cardinality free‑text columns (Name, Ticket, Cabin) risk over‑fitting, so we extract concise signals and then drop the raw text. • Name: capture the passenger title (e.g. Mr, Mrs, Miss) with a regex; titles are known strong predictors of survival. • Cabin: extract the deck letter (first character) which encodes location on the ship and is far less sparse than the full cabin code (77 % missing). • Ticket: extract any alphabetic prefix (e.g. “PC”, “A/5”) that groups tickets bought together. We also create a group‑size feature for Ticket to capture families or groups sharing a ticket. • Fare is highly right‑skewed (skew = 4.79) so we log‑transform it. • Age has ~20 % missing; we keep the column (imputation will be handled downstream) and add a missing‑indicator (default true). • Embarked, Sex and Pclass are low‑cardinality categoricals; we frequency‑encode them to give tree models a numeric representation without one‑hot explosion. • Ticket and Cabin (raw) are dropped after extracting the deck/prefix and group‑size, as they provide little additional signal beyond the engineered features. PassengerId is a pure identifier and is also dropped. No datetime columns exist. The target is binary, so we do not log‑transform it. This plan directly addresses the listed risks: class imbalance is handled by model choice, missing Age is flagged, and high‑cardinality text is reduced to compact categorical signals.

Across four iterations no CV gain was achieved (best_cv_gain stays 0.0) despite trying models and tuning, and the remaining budget allows only two more submissions and no further experiment iterations. The feature importance list shows only a few strong signals (Fare, Age) while high‑cardinality text columns (Name, Ticket, Cabin) are still raw or dropped without engineered signals. Missing‑age handling is minimal, and frequency‑encoding is only applied to a few columns. Therefore the score is limited mainly by feature engineering and possible over‑fitting of the LightGBM model.
decision.diagnosis: Score limited by (1) under‑utilised high‑cardinality text features, (2) lack of interaction/ratio features beyond simple Age/Fare, (3) possible over‑fitting of the current LightGBM hyper‑parameters (high n_estimators, low regularisation) leading to a CV‑LB gap, and (4) exhausted experiment budget preventing further model‑centric tuning. The next gain must come from richer, leakage‑free features and modest regularisation rather than more hyper‑parameter sweeps.
suggestions: Implement the full feature_plan: extract Title from Name, Deck from Cabin, and TicketPrefix from Ticket using the provided regexes; create group‑size feature for Ticket; add Age/Fare ratio; frequency‑encode Ticket, Cabin, Embarked, Sex, Pclass, Title, and the extracted TicketPrefix and CabinDeck; keep log‑transform on Fare; add missing‑indicator flags for Age (and any other column with missing values); drop raw high‑cardinality text columns (Name, Ticket, Cabin) and PassengerId; ensure no data leakage in encoding (fit encoders on training folds only).

Retrain the existing LightGBM model with the same hyper‑parameters but enable early stopping on a validation split and consider adding a modest L2 regularisation (reg_lambda 2.0) to reduce over‑fitting.
After retraining, evaluate CV mean and standard error; if CV remains ~0.84 but LB is expected to improve (gap <0.03), generate a submission file and use one of the two remaining submission slots.
If possible, run a quick sanity check with a different tree model (e.g., CatBoost with default settings) on the new feature set to compare LB performance before the final submission.
